newsitem.title: USA: Copper market rallies on Kennecott strike.
newsitem.headline: Copper market rallies on Kennecott strike.

text.p: Copper prices rose strongly Thursday after 1,800 workers at Kennecott Utah Copper Corp.'s mine and smelter walked off their jobs late Wednesday after talks on a new contract broke down.

Oil prices ended higher with traders awaiting Friday's meeting between Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary and oil industry executives to discuss possible ways to curb heating oil price spikes this winter.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange's COMEX division, December copper futures closed 2.25 cents a pound higher at 90.90 cents.
Prices jumped higher from the opening bell after news of the strike by the United Steelworkers of America at Kennecott's Utah mine and smelter, which can produce 310,000 short tons of copper a year.
Kennecott, a unit of British mining giant RTZ Corp., said Thursday it was operating the Utah facility with management and contract workers.
The union's three-year labour contract expired Sept. 30 and negotiations with Kennecott resumed during the day.
"Psychologically, the strike probably helped, but the market was maybe due for a little bit of correction anyway," said William O'Neill of Merrill Lynch.

"We can probably go a couple of weeks before it becomes a serious problem. London Metal Exchange stocks will also continue to go down for a while, but it won't be a permanent situation," O'Neill said.
"Kennecott is something that has to be watched," he said.

Union officials said the strike at Kennecott heightened tensions at Phelps Dodge Corp.'s Chino mine in New Mexico, where employees have been without contracts for more than three months. That facility has capacity of 170,000 tons.
The steelworkers union represents most hourly workers at both plants, and Chino labour talks are to resume Oct. 24.
Phelps said Chino was operating normally at full output.

At the NYMEX, November crude oil ended 25 cents higher at $25.42 a barrel, November heating oil rose 0.73 cent to close at 72.29 cents a gallon and November unleaded gasoline rose 1.08 cents a gallon to 66.53 cents.

Friday's meeting with O'Leary stems from persistent low oil product stocks. Thursday's report from the Department of Energy's Information Agency showed distillate or heating oil feedstock inventories down another 900,000 barrels last week.

Stockpiles, particularly in the Northeast, have been running substantially below last year's levels, when a severe winter led to substantial price gains. But analysts remain sceptical the government can intervene to cap prices.
"People are a little scared of this meeting tomorrow but most believe that politicians don't really have much ability to do anything," said Thomas Blakeslee, a trader at Cargill Investors Service.

Cocoa futures at the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange closed at two-month highs on indications of continuing strong demand. December cocoa ended $10 higher at $1,412 per metric ton, the contract's highest finish since Aug. 21.
The third quarter "grind" or cocoa processing demand in the Netherlands rose by 17 percent in the third quarter compared with a year ago, and British demand was up 42 percent.
Figures for the U.S. third-quarter grind are due Friday, with industry sources expecting a 3 percent to 10 percent rise.
Prudential Securities analyst Arthur Stevenson said the market's reaction to the U.S. grind figures was likely to be muted unless the number sharply differs from expectations.
"The bulk of the information is already out there after the European grinds," said Stevenson. "By definition, after their release the impact of the U.S. grind is diluted."
